context: Two education students discussing a project on outdoor learning

cues.t: Part 3. You will hear two education students, Chloe and Liam, discussing Liam's project on outdoor learning in a primary school. First you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.
Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.
Hi Chloe. Thanks for reading my draft. I'm presenting the outdoor learning project next week, and I want to be sure it makes sense.
It was really interesting. Remind me, what made you choose the topic? Was it that lecture by Dr Okafor?

No, I missed most of that, I'm afraid. And it certainly wasn't my own school days, because we hardly ever left the classroom. It came from my teaching placement. The school I was sent to had this huge garden that nobody was using, and I couldn't stop wondering what could be done with it.
How did the headteacher react? I imagine she was worried about the cost.

Actually, money wasn't an issue, because a local charity offered to pay for the equipment. And she wasn't bothered about the children getting wet or cold. What concerned her was the timetable. With so much to cover in maths and English, she felt that every hour outside was an hour lost from lessons.
That's understandable. So what did you notice once you'd started?

I expected the boys to enjoy it more than the girls, but there was no difference at all. And although they found it hard to concentrate for the first week, that soon passed. What struck me was the shy children. Pupils who'd hardly said a word in class all term started chatting to each other and asking questions.
Did the class teacher notice that too?
She did. She said it was the first time she'd heard some of those children speak in a full sentence, and she's now planning to take them outside at least once a week.

That's lovely. My one criticism is the evaluation. You say their work improved, but improved compared to what? Talking to the parents wouldn't really help, and it's too late to add more schools. What you need is to compare them with a class that stayed indoors for the same six weeks.
You're right. There's another class in the same year, so I could use their test scores.
Perfect. And what about the appendix? Are you putting in those photographs of the children?

I can't, because I never got written permission from all the parents. And the questionnaires would take up thirty pages. So I'll just include my lesson plans, since other teachers might find them useful.
Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.
Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.
Now, the section on your five activities. What did each one do for the children? Start with the minibeast hunt.

They went searching for insects under logs, and they had to record what they found. They started looking very closely, counting legs and comparing wings, and noticing tiny details they'd never have seen in a textbook.
And the den building?

People say it builds confidence, but I didn't really see that. The real gain was that they had to work as a team. Nobody could hold up the branches alone, so they learned to share out the jobs and agree on a plan.
Did they all join in?
Nearly all of them. A couple of them complained about the mud at first, but once the walls started going up, they forgot all about it.
Then there's growing vegetables.

That one was slow. For weeks there was nothing to see but soil, and at first the children kept digging up the seeds to check on them. In the end, they accepted that some things can't be hurried, and that you simply have to wait.
What about the story walk?

We stopped at different places, and the children made up a story as they went along. By the end, they were using words like rustling, damp and shadowy, which had never appeared in their writing before. Their range of language really grew.
Did you write down what they said?
Yes, I recorded the stories on my phone and typed them up later, so I've got plenty of examples to quote.
And last of all, measuring shadows.

They measured their own shadows every hour with tape measures, and then they drew charts. Children who said they hated numbers were suddenly working out differences and averages, so it was wonderful for their maths.
That's a really strong section, Liam.
That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

items.stem: Why did Liam choose outdoor learning as his topic?

options.A: He had attended a lecture about it.
options.B: He had seen unused grounds at his placement school.
options.C: He had enjoyed outdoor lessons as a pupil.

options.B: Boys enjoyed the lessons more than girls.

groups.instruction: What was the main benefit of each activity?
groups.limit: Choose FIVE answers from the box and write the correct letter, A–F, next to Questions 26–30.
